lexicon.name: Shop
lexicon.description: A small order API used to examine domain meaning, software structure, and runtime collaboration. It validates quantities and keeps accepted orders in process memory. It has no pricing, payment, inventory, authentication, or durable storage.

context.name: Ordering
context.description: Agree on which products and quantities a [[customer|customer]] requests. An [[order]] gives that request an identity, while each [[order-line]] records one requested product quantity; this example does not model prices or stock availability.

concept.name: Order
concept.description: An accepted request identified independently of its product quantities. Its [[order-line|lines]] describe what was requested, while [[checkout]] assigns the request an identity and invokes its validation before handing it to [[repository]]. Acceptance here means valid quantities, not payment or fulfillment.
concept.annotation: Creation requires at least one product with a nonempty SKU and a positive whole quantity.
concept.code-link: Order stores identity and checks the initial lines in its constructor.

concept.name: Order Line
concept.description: A product identifier and its requested quantity within an [[order]]. A line has no separate identity: its SKU and quantity describe part of the request. The order checks those values on creation and copies the supplied records so later edits to the input do not change its initial lines.
concept.code-link: The TypeScript record names a SKU and quantity.

person.name: Customer
person.description: The intended caller of [[api]], supplying the product quantities that may become an [[order]]. The fixture does not authenticate callers or provide a customer interface, so this role expresses intended use rather than a verified customer identity.
person.annotation: A customer submits the products they want to order.

system.name: Shop
system.description: The software system accepting orders through [[api]]. It gives the [[ordering]] vocabulary a small executable example: valid requests become identified orders held in process memory, without pricing, payment, inventory, authentication, or durable storage.

container.name: Shop API
container.description: A Bun application exposing POST /orders. It parses incoming JSON and delegates creation to [[checkout]], returning the accepted order with HTTP 201 or a refusal with HTTP 400. Its [[repository]] lives in the same process, so a successful response does not imply durable storage.
container.code-link: Routes a request to the checkout component and returns acceptance or refusal.

component.name: Order Handling
component.description: Creates a validated [[order]], assigns its identity, and passes it to [[repository]]. The code calls this responsibility Checkout, but it performs no payment or pricing. Validation happens during construction, so the [[reject-order|invalid-quantity path]] stops before storage.
component.code-link: Checkout is the code name for the Order Handling responsibility.

component.name: Order Repository
component.description: Stores accepted [[order|orders]] by ID in a map owned by the [[api]] process. [[checkout]] supplies each order after successful construction; restarting the process loses the stored requests, even though their callers received an acceptance response.
component.annotation: Orders are lost when the API process restarts.
component.code-link: The repository stores orders by ID in process memory.

relationship.name: contains
relationship.description: An [[order]] contains [[order-line|product quantities]] as the contents of one request. This domain membership gives the lines meaning within the order; both concepts still belong to [[ordering]], and the relationship does not change that structural parentage.
relationship.code-link: Order copies the input lines into its lines collection.

relationship.name: submits orders to
relationship.description: Clients acting in the intended [[customer]] role submit product quantities to [[api]] through POST /orders. The implementation accepts the request without checking a customer identity, so this connection describes the entry into ordering rather than authentication.
relationship.code-link: The handler accepts POST requests without authenticating a customer identity.

relationship.name: creates
relationship.description: [[checkout]] invokes the [[order]] constructor before saving the result. That constructor checks the requested lines; a failure interrupts creation and leads to [[reject-order]], leaving the repository uncalled.
relationship.code-link: Constructs Order and then calls repository.save.

relationship.name: saves accepted orders through
relationship.description: After successful validation, [[checkout]] passes the new [[order]] to [[repository]], which was supplied at application startup. This handoff retains the accepted request for the process lifetime; it does not write it to durable storage.
relationship.code-link: The call to repository.save connects these components.

relationship.name: stores
relationship.description: [[repository]] stores an accepted [[order]] under its ID for the lifetime of one [[api]] process. The ID supports lookup independently of the requested quantities, but the map provides no persistence across restarts.
relationship.code-link: Stores the supplied order under its ID.

relationship.name: dispatches orders to
relationship.description: [[api]] parses the request body and passes its product quantities to [[checkout]] for validation and creation. Parsing must succeed before this handoff; construction failures then return through the handler as HTTP 400.
relationship.code-link: The handler invokes checkout.place after parsing the JSON request body.

relationship.name: constructs and validates an order within
relationship.description: Within [[checkout]], Checkout.place invokes Order.constructor to validate the requested quantities before storage. [[order]] describes the business meaning of the resulting object; the executing responsibility remains Order Handling.
relationship.code-link: Constructs Order before calling the repository.

flow.name: Place an Order
flow.description: A valid POST /orders request reaches [[api]], which delegates to [[checkout]] to create an [[order]] and save it through [[repository]]. The caller receives the created order with HTTP 201; the accepted request remains only in process memory. [[reject-order]] explains what happens when the supplied quantities fail validation.
flow.annotation: This scenario assumes valid product quantities. Parsing or order validation failures produce HTTP 400 before the repository is called. A successful request returns the created order with HTTP 201.
flow.code-link: Routes the request and reports success or failure.
Constructs and validates Order before saving it through the repository.
Stores the validated order in process memory.
After parsing JSON, calls Checkout.place directly.
flow.step: Submit product quantities via HTTP POST /orders

flow.name: Reject Invalid Quantities
flow.description: A POST /orders request supplies a JSON array with an empty SKU or a nonpositive or fractional quantity. [[checkout]] attempts to construct an [[order]], whose validation throws; [[api]] returns HTTP 400 and [[repository]] is not called. Unlike [[place-order]], this path produces no stored order.
flow.code-link: Defines the scenario ordering and outcome.
flow.annotation: This is the domain validation path. Malformed JSON fails earlier, before dispatch; unmatched routes return HTTP 404. Neither alternate is expanded here.
flow.code-link: Attempts construction before saving the order.
Rejects invalid quantities inside the Order Handling responsibility.
Construction throws before the repository is called.
flow.step: Submit invalid product quantities via HTTP POST /orders
Construct Order and reject invalid lines
